findings.description: The decision to entrust becomes abandoning everything

contexts.japanese:
「私は、
……委ねる、決断をしました」
「………委ねる……」
「先代当主より全てを受け継いだ儀式の時のように。
……私もまた、奇跡という名の運命に身を委ねることを選びました」
ルーレットに、身を委ねたといった方が、正しいかもしれない。
私は、私たちは、……自分たちの運命さえ決められなくて。
全てを運命に託したのです。

contexts.MG:
"I decided...
...to abandon control over everything."
"...Abandon control..."
"Like the ceremony in which I inherited everything from the previous Head,
...I decided to abandon myself to the fate known as a miracle."
It may be more accurate to say that I abandoned myself to the choice of the roulette.

so we let fate decide everything for us.

...to delegate my fate."
".........Delegate it......"

......I decided to put myself in the hands of that fate called a miracle."
It may be more accurate to say that I entrusted my fate to a spin of the roulette.
I—we—could not even decide our own fate,
so we let fate decide everything for us.

findings.sourceReading: Clair decided to entrust, echoed by Lion. She entrusts herself to fate/roulette, while the narrator explicitly distinguishes this from abandoning her own fate because she approaches it with absolute will.
findings.alternative: Abandon oneself to something can validly mean surrender or entrust oneself, so the later abandon myself to fate phrases are not independently errors. Bare abandon everything and Lion bare Abandon lose that construction and state renunciation instead. The later not resigned to fate further replaces the source non-abandonment distinction with an emotional resignation distinction.

findings.sourceReading: The mystery cannot die until the detective gives it its last rites. The surrounding funeral personifies Clair and the unresolved mystery that Will must lay to rest.
findings.alternative: In the mystery genre can introduce a metagenre aphorism, and last rites preserves funeral imagery. But there can be no death makes death generally impossible in the genre, rather than making the mystery itself the subject that needs detective resolution.

contexts.UP: ......Illusions who have fulfilled their role do not leave a corpse."

findings.sourceReading: The illusion that has finished its role cannot leave even a corpse. 残せない explicitly denies the ability to leave one, with さえも emphasizing that limit. This answers the preceding claim that the pair cannot be together even as corpses.
findings.alternative: Do not leave a corpse can be a generic statement and still communicates corpse absence. It does not, however, retain the explicit inability or even emphasis, leaving voluntary non-provision or removal compatible with the wording where the source states a constraint. The neighboring no illusion can create a corpse concerns a separate twilight and only partly recovers the distinction.

findings.sourceReading: Will asks what would have happened if the man had insisted on seeing the dead face and stepped inside. Japanese does not assign that face to the addressee.
findings.alternative: Clair represents the mystery being discussed, which can motivate an interpretive possessive. The source leaves the face unassigned and explicitly calls it dead; your face removes that description and adds identity.
